newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Ozawa struggles against manipulator tag.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Ozawa struggles against manipulator tag.

text.p: Top opposition leader Ichiro Ozawa is struggling against a reputation as a master behind-the-scenes manipulator in his bid to become Japan's next prime minister.
With one week left to the October 20 general election, Ozawa's ideas to slash income tax and cut the number of civil servants have caught the imagination of much of the electorate.
But his decade-long role as a "kingmaker" in Japanese politics is holding many people back from handing the crown in person to the 54-year-old Ozawa.

Supporters say Ozawa, head of Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), does not deserve his reputation and should be praised, not dammed, for the scheming that has kept Japanese politics in turmoil throughout the 1990's.

During the period, Ozawa was credited with installing three prime ministers and bringing low his previous party, the giant Liberal Democratic Party, by bolting from it to eventually form Japan's first serious opposition party since World War two.
Critics, most of all Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's rival (LDP), say Ozawa is untrustworty, hypocritical and dedicated solely to a lust for power.

Aware of the questions about him, Ozawa in the past week has stepped out of the backroom and taken to the election trail with gusto, surprising friends and foes with his easy-going manner at the most out-of-the-way campaign stops.
"This is a man who some people said was only at ease with professional politicians," one aide gloated at the weekend as Ozawa was cheered during a speech delivered in driving rain
Besides, the aide added, he loves birds and dogs and has many of them at his home.
But the character question keeps cropping up.
"Mr Ozawa, people like your ideas but they just don't seem to like you. Why?" was one question at a weekend news conference he gave during a six-city whistlestop tour.
Ozawa was not flustered by the question.
"Of course people would rather be liked than not liked," he replied. "But for this election, voters should look at the policies of candidates, not at whether they are likeable."
Born in Ibaraki Prefecture north of Tokyo on May 24, 1942, Ozawa graduated from Keio University before running for parliament in 1969 from his late father's consituency.
Aides portray the young Ozawa as initially a reluctant politician who only took on the job out of a sense of responsibility to his father.
"He did not train to become a politician and was 27 before he made his first overseas trip," a close friend said.
The trip was to Israel when the Middle East was in turmoil and the visit had a powerful effect on Ozawa, making him aware of Japan's frail reliance on oil from the area.
But with the single-mindedness that was to later become a trademark, Ozawa, once on board, rose quickly through the LDP ranks, becoming LDP secretary-general in 1989 at the age of 47.
His organisational skills, and loyalty to those in power, saw him fill influential but unglamorous behind-the-scenes administrative posts in the LDP.
"I think this is where this mistaken mystique about him being a manipulator started," the friend said.

Ozawa played a key role in restoring the LDP's battered fortunes after the trauma of the Recruit shares-for-favours scandal, which brought down Noboru Takeshita's government and tainted a whole generation of LDP grandees.
Taking up the LDP leadership just a month after disastrous 1989 Upper House elections, Ozawa piloted the party to a decisive general election win in February 1990.
The next four years saw constant LDP infighting which culminated in Ozawa breaking completely from the party with 40 like-minded rebels who founded a new party.
At the end of 1994, he put together a grand alliance of nine non-communist parties to form Shinshinto.
Ozawa is not all manipulation and backroom deals. His 1993 bestselling book, "A Plan to Rebuild Japan," spelled out the reformist platform which is the basis of his present campaign.

In the book, which Ozawa says still hold true, he compares Japanese politics to a dinosaur with a small brain. He blames this on the Japanese traditional need to achieve consensus at all costs, which renders quick decisions impossible and ensures responsibility gets lost.
While Japan's prime minister is nominally the head of the government, he has in reality only limited power, with lawmaking largely in the hands of unelected bureaucrats.
Asked at the weekend what he would like most to achieve if elected prime minister, Ozawa replied without hesitation:
"I want politicians to have power, not bureaucrats."
